name: Submalar filler

lead: Submalar filler adds volume to the hollow beneath the cheekbones, giving a fuller or more defined lower midface and a lifted cheek contour. The change is visible after treatment.

It is a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants, which augment the midface while malar implants sit on the cheekbones. A clinician injects a gel filler, typically hyaluronic acid, into the tissue below the cheekbone, adding volume until the body gradually resorbs it. Small registered trials have tested hyaluronic acid and other fillers for midface volume and cheek augmentation.

paras: It is a short clinic treatment with little downtime. People choose it as a temporary, reversible way to try a fuller cheek contour, and repeat it as the filler is absorbed.
Asymmetry from uneven resorption or shifting is listed among the risks of cheek augmentation. Filler is eventually resorbed, so results are temporary. Fillers are given by licensed practitioners.

angle.text: Submalar filler adds volume in the hollow beneath the cheekbone for a fuller, lifted cheek contour, as a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants. The change is visible after treatment and is temporary. Small registered trials have tested fillers for midface volume.

lead: Submalar filler is an injectable filler placed in the hollow below the cheekbone to add volume to the lower midface. It is a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants, which Wikipedia describes as augmenting the midface, while malar implants sit on the cheekbones [1].

Wikipedia names hyaluronic acid products such as Restylane and Juvederm and autologous fat as materials used for cheek augmentation, and notes that fillers are eventually resorbed [1]. Registered clinical trials have tested hyaluronic acid and other fillers for midface volume and cheek augmentation [2][3].

paras: Wikipedia describes cheek augmentation as done with implants (silicone, porous polyethylene or ePTFE) or with injectables, and distinguishes malar implants (cheekbones), submalar implants (midface) and combined implants [1]. Fillers are injected rather than implanted, and the article notes that fat, although described as more permanent, still resorbs [1].
Wikipedia lists asymmetry as a risk for all forms of cheek augmentation, from uneven resorption or shifting, and temporary loss of sensation as common with implants [1].

Registered trials include a study of a hyaluronic acid product for restoration of mid-face volume deficit in 30 participants, recruiting from 2025 [2], and a small completed study of a tissue filler, SMI-01, in the nasolabial fold and cheek augmentation in 21 participants [3]. Results are not summarised in the registry entries reviewed here.
